title: GOD CALLED JERUSALEM AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE… BUT WHAT HE SAID NEXT SHOULD BRING EVERY SINNER TO TEARS
paragraphs: GOD CALLED JERUSALEM AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE… BUT WHAT HE SAID NEXT SHOULD BRING EVERY SINNER TO TEARS

The shocking prophecy of Ezekiel 16 exposes the spiritual betrayal of an entire city, the terrifying consequences of forgetting God, and the covenant mercy that points us toward Jesus Christ—the Savior who can rewrite even the most scandalous story.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you uncomfortable enough to wonder whether God is speaking about someone else… or exposing something inside you.
Ezekiel 16 is one of those chapters.
It is not a gentle bedtime story. It is not a collection of inspirational sayings meant to make everyone feel better about themselves.
It is a devastating portrait of betrayal.
A city rescued from death. A people loved beyond anything they deserved. A covenant established by the living God.
And then…
The very people God rescued turned the gifts of His kindness into instruments of rebellion.
But here is what makes this chapter almost unbearable.
God does not describe Jerusalem's idolatry merely as breaking a religious rule.
He describes it as the betrayal of a marriage.
The God who rescued her becomes the Husband she abandons.
The blessings He gives become the treasures she carries into the arms of false gods.
And the city that once lay helpless, with nobody willing to save her, begins living as though she never needed Him at all.
Before this story ends, however, God will speak words that seem almost impossible after everything Jerusalem has done.
Words about remembering His covenant.
Words about atonement.
Words that make the coming of Jesus Christ shine with extraordinary beauty.
And perhaps the most disturbing question in this entire prophecy is not what Jerusalem did thousands of years ago.
Perhaps it is this:
What have we done with the blessings God placed in our hands?
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual betrayal begins not when someone openly declares war against God…
But when someone slowly learns to enjoy His gifts while forgetting His presence.
The prophet Ezekiel was living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon when the word of the LORD came to him.

Jerusalem was facing the consequences of generations of covenant rebellion. Its leaders had repeatedly embraced injustice, idolatry, and false security. The city that carried God's name had become deeply corrupted.
And God commanded Ezekiel to confront her with her abominations.
In Ezekiel 16:2, the prophet is told:
"Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations." (KJV)
Notice something important.
God was not exposing Jerusalem because He lacked knowledge of her sin.
He was exposing Jerusalem because she had become dangerously comfortable with it.
There is a frightening condition of the human heart in which wrongdoing no longer feels wrong.
The conscience grows quiet.
The excuses grow louder.
The things that once brought conviction become normal.
And eventually, a person can become so accustomed to spiritual compromise that correction begins to sound like cruelty.
That was Jerusalem's condition.
But instead of beginning with her crimes, God begins with her history.
He takes her back to the place where everything started.
And what He reveals is heartbreaking.
Jerusalem is portrayed as an abandoned newborn.
Unwashed.
Unprotected.
Unwanted.
Left exposed in a field, with no one showing compassion.
Ezekiel 16:5 describes a child cast into the open field because nobody pitied her.
This is prophetic imagery, not a literal account of one infant's biography. God is describing Jerusalem's helpless beginnings and the grace by which He established her.
Then comes one of the most astonishing declarations in the chapter.
In Ezekiel 16:6, God says:
"Yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
בְּדָמַיִךְ חֲיִי
Bĕdamayikh ḥăyî.
Literally, the expression means, "In your blood, live!"
The image is startling.
The child has no ability to rescue herself.
She has no beauty or achievement with which to negotiate her survival.
She cannot promise future loyalty.
She cannot offer anything in return.
Yet God commands life where abandonment seemed to have pronounced death.
Live.
One word changes everything.
And although Ezekiel is speaking specifically about Jerusalem, the imagery reminds Christians of a greater truth found throughout Scripture.
Salvation begins with God's mercy, not human merit.
Ephesians 2:4–5 declares that God, rich in mercy and great love, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in sins.
Think about that.
Before you knew how to pray properly.
Before you understood theology.
Before you knew how to explain grace.
God was already the kind of Savior who shows mercy to the helpless.
Some of you reading this remember seasons when your life seemed beyond repair.
Perhaps addiction had taken more than you wanted to admit.
Perhaps pride destroyed a relationship you thought would last forever.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps your public life looked respectable while your private life was collapsing.
Or perhaps you have carried shame so long that you have forgotten what it feels like to stand before God without hiding.
Ezekiel 16 does not tell you that sin is harmless.
It tells you something more profound.
The God who exposes sin is also the God whose mercy gives life.
And Jerusalem's story does not end in the field.
God describes her growth, His covering of her nakedness, His covenant with her, and the extraordinary beauty He bestows upon her.
In Ezekiel 16:8, God declares:
"I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine." (KJV)
There is a beautiful Hebrew expression here:
וַתִּהְיִי לִי
Vattihyî lî.
"And you became mine."
These words belong to the covenant-marriage imagery of the prophecy.
God is portraying Jerusalem as someone He rescued, clothed, adorned, and bound to Himself by covenant.
Her beauty was not independent of Him.
Her honor was not self-created.
Her prosperity was not proof that she had outgrown her need for God.
Ezekiel 16:14 explains that her beauty was perfect through the splendor God had placed upon her.
And then comes the turning point.
One of the saddest sentences in the entire chapter.
"But thou didst trust in thine own beauty..." (Ezekiel 16:15, KJV)
Read that again.
She trusted in her own beauty.
The beauty God had given her.
The gifts that should have awakened gratitude became the foundation of her pride.
The blessing became more important than the Blesser.
And the heart that should have said, "Everything I have came from You," began behaving as though God were no longer necessary.
This is where the prophecy stops feeling like ancient history.
Because how many of us have done something similar?
We prayed for employment, and when God provided, our work consumed the time we once devoted to Him.
We prayed for financial stability, and when our circumstances improved, generosity became harder.
We prayed for relationships, but once those relationships entered our lives, we allowed them to determine our obedience.
We prayed for opportunities, recognition, influence, or success.
And somewhere along the way, we began measuring our worth by the very things we once begged God to provide.
Not every blessing leads to idolatry.
Not every success is evidence of pride.
But any good gift can become spiritually dangerous when we begin trusting it more than the Giver.
Jerusalem did not merely forget God.
She used what God had given her to pursue other gods.
Ezekiel describes the city taking her beautiful garments, jewelry, gold, silver, oil, incense, and food—gifts associated with God's provision—and directing them toward idolatrous worship.
The language becomes deliberately graphic.
God portrays Jerusalem as a wife pursuing other lovers.
The Hebrew verb used in Ezekiel 16:15 comes from the root:
זנה
Z-N-H, commonly represented as zanah.
The verb can describe prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness. In prophetic contexts, it is also used figuratively for religious infidelity, especially idolatry and covenant betrayal.
This distinction matters.
Ezekiel is not inviting readers to indulge in sexual scandal.
He is using shocking marriage imagery to reveal the seriousness of spiritual betrayal.
The metaphor is severe because the covenant relationship is sacred.

And the chapter's explicit language should not be softened into something harmless, nor used to shame victims of sexual abuse or betrayal. Jerusalem is the prophetic subject, and the accusations concern the city's covenant rebellion.
God is exposing the ugliness of idolatry, not treating wounded people as objects of disgust.
The accusation becomes even more devastating when Ezekiel describes the sacrifice of children.
In Ezekiel 16:20–21, Jerusalem is condemned for offering her sons and daughters in connection with idolatrous worship.
This was not merely a matter of personal preference or cultural difference.
It involved the destruction of vulnerable human lives.
The chapter also exposes the wider moral corruption of Jerusalem, including her failure to care for the poor and needy.
Ezekiel 16:49 identifies pride, abundance, complacency, and neglect of the vulnerable among the sins associated with Sodom.
That is an uncomfortable combination.
Religious rebellion.
Social injustice.
Pride.
Cruelty.
Indifference toward suffering.
All appearing within a people who claimed a covenant relationship with God.
And suddenly, we are confronted with a truth that modern Christianity cannot afford to ignore.
You can possess religious language and still be spiritually unfaithful.
You can know worship songs and still mistreat people.
You can defend biblical morality publicly while privately excusing your own cruelty.
You can condemn another person's sins while refusing to repent of your own pride.
You can appear deeply religious and still withhold compassion from someone God commands you to love.
Jesus Himself confronted this kind of hypocrisy.
In Matthew 23:23, He rebuked religious leaders who were meticulous about certain religious duties while neglecting weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith.
God has never been impressed by outward religion that refuses inward surrender.
And Ezekiel's message becomes even more piercing when God repeatedly reminds Jerusalem of something she had forgotten.
Her beginning.
Her helplessness.
Her rescue.
Her covenant.
Her dependence.
Ezekiel 16:22 declares:
"And in all thine abominations and thy whoredoms thou hast not remembered the days of thy youth..." (KJV)
She forgot.
Not because the past had ceased to exist.
But because gratitude had disappeared from her heart.
There is a kind of spiritual forgetfulness that destroys people quietly.
You forget the prayers you once prayed through tears.
You forget how desperately you once needed forgiveness.
You forget the people who carried you when you could barely stand.
You forget the mercy that met you when your life was falling apart.
And eventually, you begin treating grace as though it were something you earned.
That is a dangerous place to live.
Because when gratitude disappears, entitlement often takes its place.
And when entitlement takes over, repentance begins to feel unnecessary.
Perhaps someone reading this remembers when prayer was not a religious routine but a desperate cry.
When worship was not merely music but a response to mercy.
You remember who you were.
You remember what God brought you through.
But somewhere between surviving the storm and enjoying the sunshine, your heart drifted.
You still believe in God.
You still know the right words.
You might even still attend church.
But the closeness is gone.
The hunger has faded.
And you have become skilled at living a Christian-looking life without surrendering the places Jesus keeps asking you to open.
If that describes you, do not turn this into another opportunity to condemn yourself without returning to God.
Let the conviction do what godly conviction is meant to do.
Lead you toward repentance.
Because the purpose of biblical correction is not to make repentance seem impossible.
It is to expose what must be forsaken so that a sinner may return to the Lord.
But we must not rush past the judgment in Ezekiel 16.
Jerusalem's betrayal had consequences.
God declares that He will expose her shame and bring judgment upon her unfaithfulness.
The imagery is disturbing, including public humiliation and violence within the prophetic judgment scene.

It reflects the terrifying consequences of covenant rebellion and the historical catastrophe facing Jerusalem. It must never be used to justify domestic abuse, sexual violence, public humiliation, or cruelty toward people accused of sin.
God's judgment is not a license for human vengeance.
The chapter confronts us with the holiness of God and the seriousness of sin.
Grace does not mean evil is imaginary.
Forgiveness does not mean injustice is unimportant.
And repentance is not simply feeling emotional for a few minutes before returning to the same deliberate rebellion.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly connect genuine turning to God with a changed direction of life.
Ezekiel himself records God's appeal in Ezekiel 18:32:
"For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye." (KJV)
Turn.
And live.
The God who pronounced life over Jerusalem's helpless beginning also calls sinners to turn from the path of destruction.
And then…
Just when Ezekiel 16 seems to have exhausted every possibility of hope…
The chapter changes.
After the accusations.
After the shame.
After the announcement of judgment.
God speaks of His covenant again.
Ezekiel 16:60 says:
"Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with thee in the days of thy youth, and I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant." (KJV)
Nevertheless.
What an extraordinary word.
Not because Jerusalem's sins were insignificant.
Not because her betrayal deserved to be overlooked.
Not because repentance and justice no longer mattered.
But because God's covenant purposes were not exhausted by Jerusalem's failure.
The Hebrew text begins with:
וְזָכַרְתִּי אֲנִי
Vĕzakhartî ʾănî.
"But I myself will remember…"
The verb comes from the Hebrew root zakhar, meaning "to remember."
In this context, God's remembering is not the recovery of information He had forgotten.
It is His covenant faithfulness coming into focus.
Jerusalem had forgotten her beginnings.
But God declares that He will remember His covenant.
Do you see the contrast?
The people forgot.
God remembered.
The people betrayed.
God declared His purpose to establish an everlasting covenant.
This is not cheap grace.
The chapter still speaks of shame, remembrance, and the silencing of self-justification.
Yet its conclusion reveals that divine judgment is not the final word in God's covenant purposes.
Then Ezekiel 16:63 gives us one of the most important statements in the chapter:
"When I am pacified toward thee for all that thou hast done, saith the Lord GOD." (KJV)
The underlying Hebrew expression is:
בְּכַפְּרִי־לָךְ
Bĕkhapperî-lakh.
It comes from the Hebrew root kaphar, associated with making atonement.
A more direct rendering of the phrase is, "When I make atonement for you."
This is crucial.
The KJV's older English expression "when I am pacified" can obscure the atonement language present in the Hebrew.
The chapter does not conclude with Jerusalem successfully purchasing God's forgiveness through her own achievements.
God Himself speaks of making atonement.
And for Christians reading Ezekiel within the whole biblical story, this opens a profound connection to Jesus Christ.
We must be careful here.
Ezekiel 16 was first spoken concerning Jerusalem and God's covenant dealings with His people. It should not be treated as though every verse were a direct prediction of the crucifixion.
Yet the themes of covenant, judgment, mercy, restoration, and atonement find their fullest Christian significance in the person and saving work of Jesus.
Ezekiel later speaks of a new heart and a new spirit in Ezekiel 36:26.
Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant in which God forgives iniquity and remembers sin no more.
And at the Last Supper, Jesus declares:
"This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." (Luke 22:20, KJV)
The Greek expression is:
ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη
Hē kainē diathēkē.
"The new covenant."
Jesus does not merely offer religious inspiration.
He gives Himself.
His blood is shed.
His body is offered.
His resurrection announces that sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
And the apostle Paul declares in Ephesians 5:25:
"Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
There is something deeply moving about placing this beside Ezekiel 16.
In Ezekiel, the covenant wife is exposed as unfaithful.
In Ephesians, Christ is revealed as the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His church.
The church is not saved because she can claim a flawless history.
She is saved by the grace of the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
That does not mean every person is automatically forgiven regardless of their response to Christ.
The Gospel calls us to repentance and faith.
But it means that the door of salvation is opened through Christ's finished work, not through our ability to manufacture a spotless past.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned how to hide our failures.
Not after we finally convinced everyone that we had always been faithful.
Christ died for sinners.
And that is where this ancient prophecy begins to reach into the deepest places of a modern heart.
Because perhaps your greatest fear is not that people will discover what you have done.
Perhaps your greatest fear is that if they knew everything, they would never look at you the same way again.
You know the secret.
The compromise.
The repeated failure.
The relationship you damaged.
The truth you avoided.
The bitterness you have protected.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
And maybe you have spent years trying to outrun the memory of it.
But the Gospel does not ask you to pretend that darkness was light.
It calls you to bring your sin into the light of Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue sinning without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding from the One who alone can cleanse you.
And there is another important distinction.
If someone has sinned against you, their wrongdoing is not your shame to carry.
God's call to forgive does not require you to remain in danger, conceal abuse, or abandon the pursuit of justice.
The Gospel confronts perpetrators with repentance and protects the dignity of those who have been harmed.
Christ's mercy never makes evil good.
It makes redemption possible.
That is why the theme of this ministry is more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because Jesus erases historical facts.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because wounds instantly stop hurting.
But because through His death and resurrection, Jesus gives sinners a future that their past could never create.
A proud person can become humble.
A dishonest person can learn to walk in truth.
A bitter heart can begin to forgive.
A person enslaved by sin can discover freedom through the Son of God.
A believer who has wandered can return in repentance.
And a life once defined by rebellion can become a testimony of mercy.
That is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
That is transformation through the Gospel.
And now, I want to ask you something.
Not as a preacher standing above you.
But as one sinner speaking to another about the mercy of Jesus Christ.
What blessing has become more important to you than the God who gave it?
Is it money?
A relationship?
A reputation?
A position?
A habit?
An ambition?
An online identity?
The approval of people who cannot save your soul?
Or perhaps it is your own religious image—the exhausting need to appear spiritually strong even when you desperately need prayer.
You do not have to answer publicly with details that could expose you to harm or violate someone else's privacy.
But do not avoid answering God.
Because Ezekiel 16 is not merely about a city that committed spiritual adultery.
It is about what happens when a heart receives mercy but refuses to remember the One who gave it.
And it is about the astonishing covenant faithfulness of God, who speaks of atonement even after exposing devastating betrayal.
Maybe today is the day you stop defending the sin you know Christ is calling you to forsake.
Maybe today is the day you apologize.
The day you confess.
The day you ask for help.
The day you reopen your Bible, not to collect another religious quotation, but to hear the voice of God through His Word.
The day you stop pretending that spiritual exhaustion is the same as spiritual maturity.
The day you come back to Jesus.
Not with excuses.
Not with performances.
Not with a carefully edited version of your story.
Just with the truth.
"Lord, I have sinned. I have wandered. I have loved things more than I have loved You. Have mercy on me through Jesus Christ. Teach me to walk in Your ways again."
That is a prayer a broken heart can pray.
And the promise of Christ is not that He turns away everyone who comes carrying shame.
He says in John 6:37:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
What a Savior.
The One who knows the truth about our sin is the very One who calls us to come to Him.
Not to prove your salvation to strangers.
Not to turn your pain into a performance.
But as a simple, honest expression of your desire to draw near to Christ.
You do not have to explain everything.
Sometimes those three words are all a weary person can manage.
Your story may help another person believe that change is possible through Christ.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this article to them privately with compassion rather than accusation.
Not every person who needs this message will ever walk into a church building.
Some are sitting alone with their phones, wondering whether God still receives people who have made terrible decisions.
Some are quietly battling temptation.
Some are carrying grief.
Some are Christians who have drifted farther than they ever intended.
And some have never truly understood why Jesus died on the cross.
A simple share may place Scripture before someone who would otherwise never encounter this message.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are growing, Christians who have grown weary, and even those who are still asking questions about faith.
We are not trying to build an audience that admires religious content while remaining unchanged.
We want to point people to Jesus.
To His Word.
To repentance.
To forgiveness.
To grace.
To the kind of discipleship that shapes how we live when nobody is watching.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Christ, there is another way you can participate in its work.

Some believers may prayerfully choose to give from their regular charitable-giving budget. But Scripture does not require anyone to redirect their tithe to an online ministry, and we would never want you to neglect your family's needs or your responsibilities to your church.
The apostle Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Cheerfully.
Not under pressure.
Not out of guilt.
But out of a sincere desire to help sound biblical teaching reach more people.
These products are not the Gospel itself. They are simply additional resources and everyday reminders that can encourage biblical reflection and conversations about faith.
Our desire is that people would not merely read one powerful article and move on.
We want them to open Scripture.
To test what they read against God's Word.
To know Christ more deeply.
To grow in prayer.
To turn away from sin.
To become more compassionate, more truthful, more faithful, and more grounded in the Gospel.
You can still help by sharing biblical resources, praying for the ministry, inviting others to follow, and making good use of the free materials available.
And every genuine act of service should ultimately point people toward Him.
Now, before you leave, return with me to that abandoned child in Ezekiel 16.
Unwanted.
Helpless.
Lying in the open field.
Then the voice of God speaks.
"Live."
Years pass.
The child becomes a beautiful city.
Blessings multiply.
Pride enters.
The heart wanders.
Covenant betrayal follows.
Judgment comes.
And yet, near the end of the prophecy, God says:
"I will remember my covenant."
That is the emotional weight of Ezekiel 16.
The chapter does not minimize the scandal.
It exposes it.
It does not flatter the sinner.
It confronts the sinner.
And it does not teach that forgiveness is cheap.
It speaks of atonement.
For those of us reading this chapter on the other side of the cross, the call is clear.
Do not trust in your own beauty.
Do not worship your blessings.
Do not mistake religious appearance for covenant faithfulness.
Do not presume upon grace while refusing repentance.
And do not believe that your shame is a greater savior than Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
The crucified and risen Lord is able to forgive, cleanse, and transform those who repent and believe.
Your past may still have consequences.
Some relationships may still need repair.
Some wrongs may still require restitution.
Some wounds may need time, wise counsel, and patient healing.
But your sin does not have to remain your master.
Jesus Christ is greater.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth of Ezekiel 16 is this:

Jerusalem forgot the God who gave her life, but God spoke of a covenant mercy that her betrayal could not earn—and in Jesus Christ, sinners are called to discover the grace that only His sacrifice can provide.
If God placed every blessing He has given you on one side, and asked whether you would still love Him without those blessings…
What would your heart reveal?
Do not answer quickly.
Let that question follow you into prayer.
Let it follow you into the decisions nobody else sees.
Let it follow you into the way you treat your family, handle your money, speak to the wounded, resist temptation, and worship when life is difficult.
And when the truth about your heart hurts, remember where the Gospel directs you.
Not toward a better disguise.
Toward the Savior.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that Jerusalem forgot her first love.
It is that any of us could read her story, recognize ourselves, and still refuse to return.
The most heartbreaking betrayal is to receive everything from God's hand, then live as though His heart means nothing—and the greatest mercy is that Jesus still calls sinners to come home.
